senses.def: no, none at all (null Ahnung = no idea)

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From the noun Null (“the number zero”), from Italian nulla, from Latin nulla, feminine singular of nullus (“no, none”).

funFacts: German says null where Greek says μηδέν and English zero: the word came from Latin nullus (“none”) through Italian.
die Stunde null (“hour zero”) is the German name for the new start in May 1945.
pitfalls: The digit as a thing is a noun with a capital: die Null, eine Null (also, colloquially, “a nobody”).
subtleties: Colloquially null means “no … at all”: Ich habe null Ahnung (I have no idea).

senses.def: one (1), when counting or standing alone

examples.text: Sie hat in Mathe eine Eins.
examples.tr: She has a 1 (the top grade) in maths.

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: Contraction of eines (nominative/accusative neuter of ein), from Middle High German einez, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *ainatō, form of *ainaz (“one”).

funFacts: In German schools the grades run from 1 (sehr gut, the best) to 6 (ungenügend): eine Eins is the dream mark.
pitfalls: Before a noun it is not eins but the article ein / eine / ein with endings: ein Buch, eine Tasse, einen Stuhl.
In compound numbers: einundzwanzig (no s), but hunderteins (with s) at the end.
subtleties: Telling the time it can stand alone: Es ist eins (it is one o’clock) – but Es ist ein Uhr.

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German zwei, from Old High German zwei (neuter of zwēne). Compare Dutch twee, English two, twain. Zwei was originally the neuter form, now used for all genders; the Old High German masculine zwēne survives in early modern zween, the feminine zwō in the variant zwo.

funFacts: Old German had three words for “two”: zween (masculine), zwo (feminine), zwei (neuter). Only zwei survived – and zwo is back as a spoken variant.
zwei is the same old word as Greek δύο, Russian два and English two.
pitfalls: On the phone, on the radio and in the army people say zwo instead of zwei, so that it is not confused with drei.
subtleties: In a café the drink stays singular after the number: Zwei Kaffee, bitte (two coffees).

examples.tr: All good things come in threes.

phrases.tr: Of all good things there are three.
phrases.meaning: third time lucky – try once more

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German drī, from Old High German dri, from Proto-West Germanic *þrīʀ, from Proto-Germanic *þrīz, from Proto-Indo-European *tréyes. Compare Dutch drie, English three, Danish tre.

funFacts: drei, Greek τρία, Russian три, Latin trēs and English three all go back to Proto-Indo-European *tréyes.
pitfalls: drei and zwei sound alike on a bad line – hence zwo for two.

examples.text: Können wir unter vier Augen sprechen?

phrases.meaning: in private, just the two of us

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German vier, from Old High German fior, from Proto-West Germanic *feuwar, from Proto-Germanic *fedwōr, from Proto-Indo-European *kʷetwṓr. Compare Dutch vier, English four, Danish fire, Swedish fyra.

funFacts: unter vier Augen – “under four eyes” – means a talk between two people only.

examples.tr: Don’t be so strict this time!

phrases.meaning: to turn a blind eye, not to be too strict

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German vünf, from Old High German fimf, from Proto-West Germanic *fimf, from Proto-Germanic *fimf, from Proto-Indo-European *pénkʷe. Formal cognates include Dutch vijf, English five, Yiddish פֿינף (finf), Gothic fimf and Icelandic fimm.

funFacts: fünf and Greek πέντε (pénte) are the same Indo-European word *pénkʷe – think of the pentagon (five corners).
pitfalls: Write ü: fünf, fünfzehn, fünfzig (fuffzehn, fuffzig are Berlin speech).

examples.text: Eine Sechs ist die schlechteste Note.

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German sehs, segs, ses, from Old High German sehs, from Proto-West Germanic *sehs, from Proto-Germanic *sehs, from Proto-Indo-European *swéḱs.

funFacts: sechs is the same old word as Greek έξι, Latin sex and Russian шесть.
pitfalls: The s disappears in sechzehn (16) and sechzig (60) – not *sechszehn, *sechszig.

examples.text: Das ist für mich ein Buch mit sieben Siegeln.
examples.tr: That is a closed book to me.

phrases.meaning: something impossible to understand (from the Book of Revelation)

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German siben, from Old High German sibun, from Proto-West Germanic *sebun, from Proto-Germanic *sebun, from earlier Proto-Germanic *sebunt, from Proto-Indo-European *septḿ̥. Compare Dutch zeven, English seven.

funFacts: sieben, Greek επτά, Latin septem and Russian семь all come from Indo-European *septḿ̥.
sieben is also a verb: Mehl sieben = to sift flour.
pitfalls: The -en disappears in siebzehn (17) and siebzig (70).

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German ahte, from Old High German ahto, from Proto-West Germanic *ahtō, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōu, from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtṓw. Compare Dutch acht, English eight, Danish otte, Swedish åtta, Greek οκτώ (októ), Latin octō.

funFacts: acht and Greek οκτώ are the same word: the k of októ became ch in German (an octopus has acht Arme).
pitfalls: Do not mix it up with die Acht in Acht geben / sich in Acht nehmen (to watch out) – an unrelated word.

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Old High German niun, from Proto-Germanic *newun, from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥. Cognate with Low German negen, Dutch negen, English nine, West Frisian njoggen, Danish ni, Gothic niun.

funFacts: neun belongs with English nine and Greek εννέα (ennéa) – all from Indo-European *h₁néwn̥.
pitfalls: eu sounds like oi: neun [nɔɪ̯n].

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German zehen, from Old High German zehan, from Proto-West Germanic and Proto-Germanic *tehun (“ten”), from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥ (“ten”). Compare Dutch tien, Low German teihn, English ten, Gothic taihun.

funFacts: zehn, Greek δέκα and Latin decem share the root *déḱm̥ – German z comes from an old t (compare English ten).
pitfalls: The teens end in -zehn (dreizehn), the tens in -zig (dreißig) – do not mix them.

examples.tr: A football team has eleven players.

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German eilf, eilef, einlif, from Old High German einlif, from Proto-Germanic *ainalif, a compound of *ainaz and *-lif. Until the 19th century usually written eilf. Compare Dutch elf, English eleven, Danish elleve.

funFacts: elf (like English eleven) is “one left over” after counting to ten; zwölf is “two left over”.
die Elf is also the football team (eleven players): die deutsche Elf.
pitfalls: False friend: German elf is the number 11; the fairy creature is der Elf / die Elfe.

examples.tr: It is five to twelve – high time to act!

phrases.meaning: at the last moment; high time to do something

synonyms.nuance: a dozen – a group of twelve, used for things (ein Dutzend Eier)

etymology.text: From Middle High German zwölf, zwolf, zwelf, zwelif, from Old High German zwelif, from an original *twelif, from Proto-Germanic *twalif. Compare Dutch twaalf, English twelve, Norwegian and Danish tolv.

funFacts: zwölf is the last number with a name of its own; from 13 on German builds the numbers from units + zehn.
pitfalls: Write ö: zwölf, not *zwolf.

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German dreizehen, from Old High German drīzehan, akin to Old Saxon thriutein. Ultimately from Proto-Germanic *þritehun. Equivalent to drei + zehn. Compare Dutch dertien, English thirteen, Danish tretten.

funFacts: Freitag, der Dreizehnte – Friday the 13th – is an unlucky day for superstitious Germans too.
pitfalls: Built like English: the unit first, then -zehn (drei + zehn = dreizehn).

examples.text: Ich bin vierzehn Tage in Berlin.
examples.tr: I am in Berlin for two weeks.

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German vierzehen, from Old High German fiorzehan, from Proto-Germanic *fedurtehun. Equivalent to vier + zehn. Compare Dutch veertien, English fourteen, Danish fjorten.

funFacts: vierzehn Tage (fourteen days) is the everyday German for “two weeks, a fortnight”.
pitfalls: Built like English: the unit first, then -zehn (vier + zehn = vierzehn).

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German vünfzehen, from Old High German fimfzehan, from Proto-Germanic *fimftehun. Equivalent to fünf + zehn. Compare Dutch vijftien, English fifteen, Danish femten.

funFacts: In Berlin you hear fuffzehn; Wiktionary also lists fuchzehn.
pitfalls: Built like English: the unit first, then -zehn (fünf + zehn = fünfzehn).

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German seh(s)zehen, from Old High German seh(s)zehan, from Proto-Germanic *sehstehun. Equivalent to sechs + zehn. Compare Dutch zestien, English sixteen, Danish seksten.

funFacts: sechzehn drops the s of sechs: sech-zehn. The spelling sechszehn is obsolete.
pitfalls: Not *sechszehn: the s of sechs is dropped.
Built like English: the unit first, then -zehn (sechs + zehn = sechzehn).

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German sibenzehen, from Old High German sibunzehan, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntehun. Equivalent to sieben + zehn. Compare Dutch zeventien, English seventeen, Danish sytten.

funFacts: siebzehn drops the -en of sieben; siebenzehn is archaic.
pitfalls: Not *siebenzehn: the -en of sieben is dropped.
Built like English: the unit first, then -zehn (sieben + zehn = siebzehn).

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German ahzehen, from Old High German ahtozehan, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōutehun. Equivalent to acht + zehn. Compare Dutch achttien, English eighteen, Danish atten.

funFacts: In Germany you come of age mit achtzehn – at eighteen.
pitfalls: Built like English: the unit first, then -zehn (acht + zehn = achtzehn).

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German niunzëhen, from Old High German niunzehan, from Proto-Germanic *newuntehun. Equivalent to neun + zehn. Compare Dutch negentien, English nineteen, Danish nitten.

funFacts: Like English nineteen: the unit first, then -zehn.
pitfalls: Built like English: the unit first, then -zehn (neun + zehn = neunzehn).

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German zweinzec, from Old High German zweinzug, from Proto-Germanic *twaintigaz, *twai tigiwiz. Cognate with Dutch twintig, English twenty, Danish tyve. The form zwanzig goes back to dialects that had early on lowered Middle High German -ei- to [aɪ̯]; elsewhere the contraction yielded zwenzig, which waned around 1700.

funFacts: 21 is einundzwanzig – “one-and-twenty”: German says the units first, like Arabic and old English (four-and-twenty blackbirds).
pitfalls: Not *zweizig: twenty is zwanzig.
From 21 on, the unit comes first: einundzwanzig, zweiundzwanzig … neunundzwanzig – written as one word.

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German drīzic, from Old High German drīzzug, from Proto-Germanic *þrīz tigiwiz. Equivalent to drei + -zig.

pitfalls: The only ten with -ßig instead of -zig: dreißig (Swiss spelling dreissig).
The tens end in -zig (-ßig in dreißig); the unit comes first in between: einunddreißig = 31.

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German vierzic, from Old High German fiorzug, from Proto-Germanic *fedwōr tigiwiz, equivalent to vier + -zig.

funFacts: -zig is the old Germanic word for “ten(s)”, the same element as English -ty (forty, fifty).
pitfalls: vier + zig: vierzig; 44 = vierundvierzig.
The tens end in -zig (-ßig in dreißig); the unit comes first in between: einundvierzig = 41.

examples.tr: The man over there is fifty.

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German vünfzic, from Old High German fimfzug, from Proto-Germanic *fimf tigiwiz. Equivalent to fünf + -zig.

pitfalls: Colloquially fuffzig or fuchzig (Wiktionary lists both).
The tens end in -zig (-ßig in dreißig); the unit comes first in between: einundfünfzig = 51.

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German seh(s)zec, from Old High German sehszug, from Proto-Germanic *sehs tigiwiz. Equivalent to sechs + -zig.

pitfalls: Not *sechszig: the s of sechs is dropped, as in sechzehn.
The tens end in -zig (-ßig in dreißig); the unit comes first in between: einundsechzig = 61.

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German sibenzec, from Old High German sibunzug, from Proto-Germanic *sebuntēhundą. Equivalent to sieben + -zig.

pitfalls: Not *siebenzig: the -en of sieben is dropped, as in siebzehn.
The tens end in -zig (-ßig in dreißig); the unit comes first in between: einundsiebzig = 71.

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German ahzec, from Old High German ahtozug, from Proto-Germanic *ahtōutēhundą. Equivalent to acht + -zig.

pitfalls: acht + zig, with one t: achtzig.
The tens end in -zig (-ßig in dreißig); the unit comes first in between: einundachtzig = 81.

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German niunzec, from Old High German niunzug, from Proto-West Germanic *neun tigiwi. Equivalent to neun + -zig.

pitfalls: neun + zig: neunzig; 99 is neunundneunzig.
The tens end in -zig (-ßig in dreißig); the unit comes first in between: einundneunzig = 91.

profile.feeling: The number a hundred, one hundred.

examples.tr: There are a hundred books here.

examples.text: Ich bin mir hundert Prozent sicher.
examples.tr: I am a hundred percent sure.

phrases.tr: to come from the hundredth to the thousandth
phrases.meaning: to digress, to go off on one tangent after another

profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German hundert, ultimately from Proto-Germanic *hundaradą, from *hundą (< Proto-Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm) + *radą (“count”).

funFacts: The hund- of hundert is Indo-European *ḱm̥tóm, the same root as Latin centum, Greek εκατό and Russian сто.
pitfalls: No ein needed: hundert = 100; einhundert is used for clarity (cheques, 101 = hunderteins).
subtleties: 101 = hunderteins, 121 = hunderteinundzwanzig: one word, the hundreds first, then units-and-tens.

profile.feeling: The number a thousand, one thousand.
profile.synonymsNone: A number has no synonym; only the figure itself.

etymology.text: From Middle High German tūsunt, from Old High German dūsunt, from Proto-West Germanic *þūsundi, from Proto-Germanic *þūsundī. Compare Old Saxon thūsund, Dutch duizend, English thousand, Danish tusind.

funFacts: tausend and Russian тысяча (tysjača) are related: this word for “thousand” is shared by the Germanic and the Balto-Slavic languages.
pitfalls: German writes thousands with a point and decimals with a comma: 1.000 = one thousand, 1,5 = one and a half.
subtleties: tausendmal = a thousand times; Tausende von Leuten = thousands of people (noun, capital T).

profile.feeling: A large amount or number – viel for “much”, viele for “many”.

senses.def: many (viele, with a plural noun); much, a lot of (viel, with a singular uncountable noun)
much, a lot (as an adverb: Er arbeitet viel)

examples.text: Auf dem Markt sind viele Leute.
examples.tr: There are a lot of people at the market.
I have a lot of time today.

phrases.meaning: too many cooks spoil the broth

synonyms.nuance: a lot of, loads of (eine Menge Leute)
numerous – an adjective of written style (zahlreiche Gäste)

etymology.text: From Middle High German vil, vile, from Old High German filu (“many”), from Proto-West Germanic *felu, from Proto-Germanic *felu, from Proto-Indo-European *pleh₁-.

funFacts: viel and Greek πολύ (polý, “much”) are related through Indo-European – poly- in English words is the Greek twin of viel.
pitfalls: viel + a singular uncountable noun (viel Papier, viel Zeit), viele + a plural (viele Bücher).
The comparative is mehr, which never takes an ending: mehr Bücher, mehr Zeit.
subtleties: Vielen Dank is a set phrase (Dank is masculine: accusative vielen Dank).
After an article it takes adjective endings: die vielen Leute (all those people).

override.pos: Wiktionary files wenig only as an adjective; like viel (which Wiktionary files as a determiner) it is used here as a quantifier before a noun – wenig Zeit, wenige Leute (Duden: Indefinitpronomen)

profile.feeling: Not much, not many – often with a note of “too little”.

senses.def: few (wenige, with a plural noun); little, not much (wenig, with a singular uncountable noun)
little, not much (as an adverb: Er isst wenig)

examples.text: Heute sind nur wenige Leute hier.
examples.tr: Only a few people are here today.

synonyms.nuance: not much / not many – the everyday way to say it

etymology.text: From Middle High German weinec, wēnec (“marginal”), from Old High German *weinag, wēnag (“miserable”), from Proto-Germanic *wainagaz. Cognate with Dutch weinig, Yiddish ווייניק (veynik).

funFacts: wenig once meant “miserable, pitiable” (Old High German wēnag); its ē came from a blend with Old High German wē (“woe”) – the same word as English woe.
pitfalls: wenig (little) ≠ ein wenig (a little): Ich habe wenig Zeit (hardly any) – Ich habe ein wenig Zeit (some).
wenig + singular uncountable, wenige + plural: wenig Papier, wenige Stühle.
subtleties: In everyday speech nicht viel / nicht viele is more common than wenig / wenige.
weniger is both the comparative (weniger Leute = fewer people) and the genitive plural form – the context tells them apart.

senses.def: a little, a bit (of something): ein bisschen Papier, ein bisschen Zeit
a bit, somewhat (before an adjective or verb: ein bisschen müde)

examples.tr: Here is a bit of paper.

collocations.tr: not a bit, not at all

synonyms.nuance: a little – the same, more careful or written

etymology.text: bisschen: adverbialized noun Bisschen, from Bissen (“a bit, bite”) + -chen (diminutive suffix).

funFacts: ein bisschen is literally “a little bite” – Bissen (bite) + -chen, just like English a bit comes from bite.
pitfalls: Write -ss-: bisschen (the old spelling bißchen was replaced in the 1996 reform).
bisschen does not decline: mit ein bisschen Glück.
subtleties: ein bisschen softens a request or criticism: Das ist ein bisschen teuer (that’s a bit expensive).

profile.feeling: A little – a shade more careful or written than ein bisschen.

senses.def: a little (of something): ein wenig Papier, ein wenig Zeit

examples.tr: There is a little paper over there.

examples.text: Haben Sie ein wenig Zeit für mich?
examples.tr: Do you have a little time for me?

etymology.text: ein + wenig; wenig from Middle High German weinec, wēnec, from Old High German *weinag, wēnag (“miserable”).

pitfalls: ein wenig (a little, some) is positive; wenig alone (little) is negative.
subtleties: In speech ein bisschen is far more common; ein wenig sounds polite or bookish.

profile.feeling: Everybody, every one of them – the whole group.

senses.def: all (with a plural noun: alle Kinder); everybody (alone: Alle sind da)
used up, gone (only after sein: Die Milch ist alle)

phrases.text: Alle für einen, einer für alle.
phrases.tr: All for one, one for all.
phrases.meaning: the motto of solidarity (the Three Musketeers)

synonyms.nuance: every, each – singular and one by one (jedes Kind)
all, the whole set – official style

etymology.text: Inflected form of all, from Middle High German al, from Old High German al, from Proto-West Germanic *all, from Proto-Germanic *allaz.

funFacts: all and English all are the same Germanic word *allaz.
pitfalls: alle is plural: alle Kinder sind …; “everything” is alles (singular): Alles ist gut.
Dative plural allen: mit allen Freunden.
subtleties: It can stand after the verb: Wir sind alle hier (we are all here).
Before the article: alle die Kinder is rare; say alle Kinder or all die Kinder.

override.meaning: Wiktionary files einige as an inflection of einig, whose determiner sense is “some, a few”; the plural einige is the form used before nouns

profile.feeling: Some, a few – a small but real number.

senses.def: some, a few, several (with a plural noun)

synonyms.nuance: a couple of, a few – the everyday word (ein paar Leute)
several – more than two, stressing the number

etymology.text: Plural of einig, from Middle High German einec, from Old High German einag, einīg, from Proto-West Germanic *ainag. More at English any.

funFacts: einig- is the German twin of English any (Proto-West Germanic *ainag, from ein, “one”).
pitfalls: einige is plural: einige Bücher. With an uncountable noun German says etwas: etwas Papier (some paper).
subtleties: Singular einiges means “quite a lot (of things)”: Ich weiß einiges darüber.

override.meaning: Wiktionary files manche as an inflection of manch (“many a; many; some”); the plural manche is the form used before nouns

profile.feeling: Some – but not all: it contrasts with the others.

senses.def: some (of a group, as opposed to the others), quite a few

synonyms.nuance: some, a few – just a small number, no contrast

etymology.text: Plural of manch, from Middle High German manec, from Old High German manag. Cognate with Dutch menig, English many, Polish mnogi.

funFacts: manch is English many: Old High German manag. The original g survives in mannigfaltig (manifold).
pitfalls: manche means “some, but not all” – it is not “many” even though it is the same word as English many.
subtleties: Singular manch- is literary: mancher Mann (many a man), manches Mal (many a time).
